title: Detection of Search Threat Vendor Data
shortTitle: Detection of Search Threat Vendor Data
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary review of threat intelligence vendor publications, incident reports and security blogs to learn which behaviours are currently detected and which tools are tracked. The attacker adjusts tradecraft to avoid published indicators, so the value of this detection is early warning that a specific report is being studied before a campaign begins. The telemetry that helps is access logging for gated or watermarked reports, tracking pixels and canary links embedded in documents, and query auditing inside a threat intelligence platform. It fails in practice because most reading happens on public sites with no authentication, leaving only the canary and watermark signals to work with.

beginner.definition: Threat intelligence vendors publish reports about attacks. These reports describe how the attacker worked and which tools were used. Some attackers read them to learn what defenders can see. This detection looks for signs that restricted or watermarked reports are being read by the wrong people.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker knows which behaviour you detect, they will change it. Published research therefore teaches attackers as well as defenders. You cannot stop anyone reading a public blog. What you can do is mark the documents that only your own staff should read, and watch for their use. A canary link inside a restricted report tells you when a copy has been opened. That warning is valuable because it arrives before the next campaign, not after it.
howItWorks: You add a unique tracking link or image to each restricted report that you publish or share.
The link points at a server you control, which records every request that it receives.
The detection reads those records and matches each identifier to the document and the intended reader.
It also reviews access logs for gated report pages and for the threat intelligence platform.
An access from outside the named reader group, or from an unexpected country, raises an alert.
An analyst then decides whether the document leaked or was shared by mistake.
beginner.example: Think of a school register that only teachers may read. Each copy of the register has a tiny hidden mark in the corner, and every copy has a different mark. If a page appears in the wrong hands, the school can tell which copy it came from. Nobody is stopped from reading, but the owner of the copy is known. Your detection uses the same idea. A unique link inside a restricted report is that hidden mark. The request log tells you exactly which copy was opened and when.
takeaways: Published research teaches attackers which behaviours to avoid.
A unique link inside a document shows which copy was opened.
Watermark warnings give early notice before the next campaign.

objectives: Explain why adversaries study threat intelligence reporting.
Describe how a canary link identifies a leaked document.
Review access logs for restricted intelligence content.
Interpret a canary alert without overreacting to innocent sharing.
Recommend handling rules for restricted reports.
dataSources: Web server access logs for the tracking endpoint used by report canary links and images
Access logs from the threat intelligence platform with account, report identifier and source address
Content access records for gated report pages, including authentication and download events
Mail or collaboration logs showing restricted reports forwarded outside the named reader group
Domain name system query logs for lookups of canary host names that appear only inside a document
logic: The pattern is access to a restricted report, canary link or watermarked document by a party that is not one of the named readers. The fields that must be correlated are the document or link identifier, the account or source address that opened it, the time of access, the intended reader list and the lookup of the canary host name in the domain name system. Benign cases include a colleague forwarding a report internally, a security vendor reviewing its own published material and a web proxy that prefetches links inside a message. The malicious case is a single access from an address outside your estate, at an hour that matches no working pattern, followed by no further contact.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Restricted Report Canary Opened Outside Named Reader Group
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     url_path|contains: '/intel/canary/'
#   filter_readers:
#     src_ip|in: 'approved_analyst_ranges'
#   filter_prefetch:
#     user_agent|contains:
#       - 'preview'
#       - 'scanner'
#   condition: selection and not filter_readers and not filter_prefetch
# level: low
falsePositives: A colleague who forwards a restricted report to a teammate in another department.
A mail security gateway that follows links inside messages for reputation checks.
The vendor that wrote the report reviewing its own hosted copy from a partner address.
A conference organiser who downloads the published version of a document you also distribute.
tuningNotes: Keep one canary identifier per document and per reader, so that an alert names the exact copy that was opened. Filter the address ranges of your own analysts, of the vendor and of any mail security service that follows links automatically. Scope the rule to reports marked as restricted, and treat public material as out of scope. If you narrow the rule to external addresses only, you lose the internal leak path, so keep internal access inside a weekly report rather than in real time alerting.
